newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-GRAF'S FATHER SAYS SHE WAS UNAWARE OF TAX SCHEMES.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GRAF'S FATHER SAYS SHE WAS UNAWARE OF TAX SCHEMES.

text.p: The father of tennis star Steffi Graf told a German court on Thursday he had kept his daughter in the dark about her finances but denied tax fraud.

The court said Steffi, the world women's number one, had declined to testify at her father's trial because she did not want to incriminate herself. As her father answered tax evasion charges, she was competing in the U.S. open in New York.
Peter Graf, a former used car salesman, blamed poor health, poor guidance and broken promises from local authorities for the tax scandal that brough his arrest 13 months ago.
"I was a physical wreck," he said. "Everything was flying over my head and I didn't have any strength left.

"There was extreme pressure on me because of the permanent travelling," he added, at times on the verge of tears. "I had been totally unprepared (for my daughter's success). I was overwhelmed and exhausted."
Having spent 13 months in investigative custody, Peter Graf faces a possible 10-year jail sentence if convicted of evading 19 million marks ($13 million) in taxes from the late 1980s.

Hours before his court appearance, his daughter, herself still under investigation in the affair, advanced to the semifinals at the U.S. Open. She admitted her mind was thousands of miles away in the Mannheim high court.
Graf, 58, who accompanied his daughter to tournaments around the world, was arrested last year because prosecutors feared he would flee the country.
He and his lawyers again pleaded for his release.
"You and I will be able to go to our homes and relax tonight, but Herr Graf will be brought back to his windowless cell in the basement of a jail," said attorney Franz Salditt.
Graf said he had always taken responsibility for his daughter's finances.
"Our daughter was completely unaware (of her tax situation) until 1995," he said. "In any case, all the back taxes have now been paid."

Wearing a light green suit and looking relaxed, Peter Graf smiled briefly as he entered a side door to the courtroom in the southwest German city of Mannheaim, but his smile disappeared as camera teams and photographers trained their lights on him.
Prosecutors read an 18-page summary of the 237-page charge sheet detailing some 42 million marks ($28 million) worth of undeclared income between 1989 and 1993.
Peter Graf read his statement and told the court he would refrain from any further comment during the course of the trial.

He said he had been close to moving his family abroad at one point to avoid high German taxes, but decided to stay because "my roots are here in Germany" and because local political leaders had assured him of tax relief for his daughter.

"I knew that such sporting achievements only last a short time and I knew I had to try to set aside financial reserves," Graf said. "It became apparent to me that taxes in Germany and abroad could eat everything up.

"Some sports stars solve this problem by emigrating," he said. "I was preparing for such an exit but my roots are here in Germany, and through conversations with political leaders I was given assurances that her taxes would be assessed with understanding. I was promised that emigration would not be necessary."
Graf said he had never felt good about a complicated tax-saving scheme in the Netherlands set up by advisers.
He said he had erred by delaying decisions on sorting out the tax affairs and by failing to see that promises made by political leaders would not be respected by tax collectors.

"I could have put everything right back in 1991 if the tax authorities had warned me of the criminal consequences," Graf said. "It would have been a shock and I would have reacted then." ($1=1.4816 Mark)
